title: Oxygen therapy and respiratory care
blurb: Give oxygen to a prescribed target with the right device, avoid the traps of pulse oximetry, and manage nebulisers, peak flow and breathlessness safely.
question: Mr Harrow, 71, has COPD and has needed ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory failure before. He arrives breathless with SpO2 85% on air and no blood gas result yet. Which oxygen device and target are appropriate?

teach.h: Oxygen is a medicine with a target
teach.body: Oxygen treats hypoxaemia (low oxygen in the blood), not breathlessness itself. The BTS guideline says prescribe it to a target saturation range, not a fixed flow, choose a device to reach that range, and adjust up or down to stay in it. Too little harms the brain, heart and kidneys; too much can cause dangerous carbon dioxide retention in people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. Plain English: aim for the range, not for 100%.
teach.cite: BTS guideline for oxygen use in adults (2017)

teach.caption: In people with COPD, the target should be guided by previous blood gases where available. Some carry an oxygen alert card stating their target.

Flow

teach.caption: BTS 2017. Always read the percentage and the minimum flow printed on the Venturi valve.

children.label: Nasal cannulae 2–6 L/min or mask 5–10 L/min

teach.body: Oxygen should be prescribed on the drug chart or electronic system to a target range, and a target should be prescribed for every patient admitted to hospital so it is ready if needed. In an emergency, give oxygen immediately and document it, then obtain the prescription. Sign for oxygen on each drug round. Reduce it in stable patients and stop it once they stay in or above the target on air, but leave the target prescription in place in case they deteriorate.

Record every SpO2 with whether the person is on air or on a named device and flow rate. Oximeters can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin (NICE NG253, CG103). They cannot detect a rising carbon dioxide level. In carbon monoxide poisoning the reading can look normal, so give high-flow oxygen by reservoir mask aiming for 100%, whatever the reading. Poor perfusion, cold fingers and movement also cause unreliable readings.
teach.cite: BTS 2017 (E6, T2); RCUK ABCDE; NICE NG253

teach.caption: BTS R1–R2. Do not let hypoxaemia occur during nebulisation: hypoxaemic patients keep their oxygen.

teach.h: Peak flow, inhalers, humidification and suction
items: Peak flow: stand or sit upright (the same way each time), take three readings with a short rest between, and record the highest.
Inhalers: help the person use their own reliever, with a spacer if available (RCUK first aid). Check their technique.
Humidification: consider a large-volume humidifier for high flows or longer-term oxygen, especially if sputum retention is a problem (BTS).
Suction: only when secretions cannot be cleared by coughing, using local policy, with oxygen and SpO2 monitoring throughout.
Restlessness or new agitation: look for hypoxia first (NICE CG103) before assuming it is behavioural.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Harrow in the acute medical unit
items: History: COPD with previous hypercapnic failure; SpO2 85% on air, RR 28, no blood gas yet.
The nurse gives oxygen via a 24% Venturi mask at 2–3 L/min, aiming for 88–92%, and asks for an urgent blood gas and medical review.
Ten minutes later SpO2 is 95%: above his target, so she reduces the oxygen and rechecks, rather than leaving it.
His salbutamol nebuliser is driven by compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae to keep him at 88–92%; afterwards his Venturi mask goes back on.
Each SpO2 entry records '24% Venturi' or the flow rate, and NEWS2 uses Scale 2 once prescribed.

teach.text: Two opposite traps. Never leave a hypoxaemic person with COPD without oxygen 'because of CO2': give controlled oxygen to 88–92%. But do not let them sit at 96–98% either: above target means reduce the oxygen.

items: Prescribe to a target: 94–98% for most, 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure.
Devices: cannulae 2–6 L/min, simple mask 5–10 L/min, Venturi 24% or 28%, reservoir 15 L/min.
In an emergency give oxygen first, document and get it prescribed afterwards.
Oximetry: record device and flow; overestimates in darker skin; misses CO2 and carbon monoxide.
Nebulisers: oxygen-driven over 6 L/min in asthma; air-driven plus cannulae in hypercapnic risk.

summary: You can now give oxygen to the right target with the right device, wean it safely and record it correctly. You understand the limits of pulse oximetry and can manage nebulisers, peak flow, humidification and breathlessness in line with BTS guidance.

A.q: Mrs Rowe, 60, has pneumonia and no lung disease. Her SpO2 is 90% on air; she is not critically ill. Which device is the most appropriate starting choice?
options: Reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Nasal cannulae at 2–6 L/min
24% Venturi mask at 2–3 L/min
Simple face mask at 1–2 L/min
A.why: BTS: for hypoxaemic patients not at risk of hypercapnic failure, start with nasal cannulae at 2–6 L/min (or a simple face mask at 5–10 L/min) and aim for 94–98%.

whyNot.0: A reservoir mask is for critically ill patients or SpO2 below 85%.
whyNot.2: A 24% Venturi is designed for controlled oxygen in hypercapnic risk, not for her.
whyNot.3: A simple face mask needs at least 5 L/min; lower flows risk rebreathing carbon dioxide.

A.q: Mr Kelly, 45, is brought in after a faulty boiler at home and carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected. His oximeter reads 98%. Which oxygen approach does BTS guidance describe?
options: Aim for 94–98% with nasal cannulae
Aim for 88–92% with a Venturi mask
Withhold oxygen while SpO2 reads 98%
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min aiming for 100%
A.why: BTS E6: carboxyhaemoglobin can produce an apparently normal oximetry reading, so aim at 100% saturation using a reservoir mask at 15 L/min irrespective of the oximeter reading.

whyNot.0: The usual target does not apply; the oximeter reading is misleading in carbon monoxide poisoning.
whyNot.1: There is no hypercapnic risk here, and controlled low oxygen would undertreat him.
whyNot.2: A normal reading is falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide poisoning.

A.q: A nurse is teaching Ms Ali, 24, who has asthma, to record her peak flow. How should she position herself?
options: Stand or sit upright, the same way each time
Lie flat to relax her chest muscles
Lean forward with her arms on a table
Lie on her left side with knees bent
A.why: Asthma + Lung UK: stand or sit upright, choose what is most comfortable and do it the same way each time; take three readings and record the highest.

whyNot.1: Lying flat reduces the force of expiration and gives lower readings.
whyNot.2: Leaning on a table may ease breathlessness but is not the standard measuring position.
whyNot.3: Side-lying is not a recommended position for peak flow.

B.q: Ms Ade, 30, has acute asthma with SpO2 91%. A salbutamol nebuliser is prescribed. How should it be driven, according to BTS?
options: By compressed air, with no oxygen given
By oxygen at a flow of more than 6 L/min
By oxygen at 2 L/min through the nebuliser
By air, adding oxygen if SpO2 drops below 85%
B.why: BTS R1: for asthma, nebulisers should be driven by piped oxygen or a cylinder with a high-flow regulator capable of more than 6 L/min.

whyNot.0: She is hypoxaemic; BTS says do not allow hypoxaemia during nebulisation.
whyNot.2: 2 L/min is too low to drive a nebuliser effectively.
whyNot.3: Air-driven nebulisers are for hypercapnic risk, and waiting for 85% allows dangerous hypoxaemia.

B.q: Mr Nye, 66, has recovered from pneumonia and now keeps an SpO2 of 96% on air. What should happen to his oxygen prescription?
options: Stop oxygen; keep the target range prescribed
Stop oxygen and cancel the prescription
Continue 1 L/min for comfort overnight
Change to a 28% Venturi mask to wean
B.why: BTS: discontinue oxygen once the patient can maintain saturation within or above target on air, but leave the target range prescription in place in case of future deterioration and to guide NEWS2.

whyNot.1: BTS advises keeping the target prescription so oxygen can be restarted correctly if he deteriorates.
whyNot.2: Oxygen is not prescribed for comfort when saturation is in range on air.
whyNot.3: A Venturi mask is not needed; he no longer needs oxygen.

B.q: Mr Ibe, 78, is a day after surgery. He becomes suddenly restless and is pulling at his face mask; his SpO2 is 86%. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative
Raise the bed rails to keep him safe
Complete a 4AT assessment before anything else
Reapply his oxygen and assess for hypoxia
B.why: Restlessness can be a sign of hypoxia. RCUK and NICE CG103 direct you to assess and treat hypoxia (A and B) before attributing behaviour to delirium or giving sedation.

whyNot.0: Sedating a hypoxic person can worsen breathing and hides the cause.
whyNot.1: Bed rails do not treat the cause and can cause harm in an agitated person.
whyNot.2: Delirium screening matters, but hypoxia must be treated first.

C.q: Mr Harrow, 71, has COPD and previous hypercapnic respiratory failure. He arrives breathless with SpO2 85% on air; no blood gas is yet available. What is the most appropriate initial oxygen?
options: Reservoir mask at 15 L/min, target 94–98%
24% Venturi at 2–3 L/min, target 88–92%
Nasal cannulae at 6 L/min, target 94–98%
No oxygen until blood gases are known
C.why: BTS: before blood gases are available in hypercapnic risk, use a 24% Venturi at 2–3 L/min (or 28% at 4 L/min, or nasal cannulae at 1–2 L/min) aiming for 88–92%.

whyNot.0: High-concentration oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia in someone with previous hypercapnic failure.
whyNot.2: 6 L/min with a 94–98% target is too much for his risk.
whyNot.3: Withholding oxygen leaves him dangerously hypoxaemic; controlled oxygen is needed now.

C.q: On a ward, Mrs Quinn, 58, with no lung disease, becomes acutely breathless with SpO2 84%. No oxygen is prescribed and the doctor is 10 minutes away. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait for the doctor to prescribe it first
Give a 24% Venturi until the doctor arrives
Wait for a blood gas result before starting
Start oxygen now; get it prescribed after
C.why: BTS S2: in sudden illness oxygen must be started immediately and documented, with the prescription obtained afterwards. With SpO2 below 85%, a reservoir mask at 15 L/min is the starting device.

whyNot.0: The lack of a prescription should never stop oxygen being given in an emergency.
whyNot.1: 24% Venturi is for hypercapnic risk; she needs high-concentration oxygen.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a blood gas leaves her hypoxaemic.

C.q: Mrs Ford, 80, has needed oxygen at high flow for several days and is struggling to clear thick sputum. Which measure does BTS guidance suggest considering?
options: A large-volume oxygen humidifier
A simple face mask at 2 L/min
Stopping oxygen overnight to rest
Raising the flow to loosen secretions
C.why: BTS: consider a large-volume oxygen humidifier for patients needing high flow rates or longer-term oxygen, especially if sputum retention is a problem.

whyNot.1: A simple mask below 5 L/min risks carbon dioxide rebreathing and does not humidify.
whyNot.2: Stopping oxygen overnight risks hypoxaemia and does not help secretions.
whyNot.3: Flow is set to reach the target saturation, not to loosen sputum.

reteach.title: A thermostat, not a tap
reteach.question: Think of oxygen like a thermostat set to a range. What do you do when the reading is below, inside or above it?

blocks.body: The prescription sets the range: 94–98% for most people, 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic failure. Below the range: increase oxygen or change device and call for review. Inside: keep going and monitor. Above: reduce. On air and in range: stop, but keep the target prescribed.

blocks.text: A simple face mask below 5 L/min is unsafe: the person can rebreathe carbon dioxide. Use nasal cannulae for low flows.

explain.body: 94–98% for most acutely ill adults; 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, guided by previous blood gases and any oxygen alert card.

test.q: What target saturation does BTS guidance set for a person at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
test.why: BTS: aim for 88–92% in people with COPD or other known risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure.

whyNot.0: 94–98% is for people not at risk of hypercapnic failure.
whyNot.1: 92–96% is not a BTS target range.
whyNot.3: 85–88% is below the target and leaves the person hypoxaemic.

explain.body: Nasal cannulae 2–6 L/min; simple face mask 5–10 L/min; Venturi 24% at 2–3 L/min or 28% at 4 L/min; reservoir mask 15 L/min.

test.q: What flow range does BTS give for a simple face mask?
options: 1–2 L/min
2–3 L/min
15 L/min
5–10 L/min
test.why: BTS: simple face mask at 5–10 L/min.

whyNot.0: 1–2 L/min is a nasal cannula flow for hypercapnic risk; too low for a mask.
whyNot.1: 2–3 L/min is the flow for a 24% Venturi mask.
whyNot.2: 15 L/min is the flow for a reservoir mask.

explain.body: Prescribe to a target range rather than a fixed flow or concentration; sign each drug round; give immediately in an emergency and document.

test.q: According to BTS, how should oxygen be prescribed?
options: As a fixed flow rate in L/min
As a fixed percentage of oxygen
As a target saturation range
As needed, with no set target
test.why: BTS: prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range rather than a fixed concentration or FiO2, and sign the drug chart.

whyNot.0: A fixed flow does not adjust to the person's changing needs.
whyNot.1: A fixed percentage is not how BTS recommends prescribing.
whyNot.3: Oxygen without a target risks under- or over-treatment.

explain.body: Record air or device and flow. Overestimates in darker skin; cannot detect hypercapnia; reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning; unreliable with poor perfusion or movement.

test.q: In a person with darker skin, how might a pulse oximeter reading differ from their true saturation?
options: It may read lower than the true value
It may read higher than the true value
It will not display any reading
It reads the same as in lighter skin
test.why: NICE NG253 and CG103: pulse oximeters can overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, so the reading may be higher than the true value.

whyNot.0: The documented concern is overestimation, not underestimation.
whyNot.2: Oximeters still give readings; the issue is accuracy.
whyNot.3: NICE warns that accuracy differs; overestimation has been reported.
